WA001-048----:
On the edge of a terrace of a N-facing slope of hills, on the W side of the mountain road known as ‘The Mayor’s Walk’, overlooking the Suir river valley. There is a sheer fall of 3-4m to the valley floor c. 1-2m to the N. There are very good to extensive views to the N, E and W with Slievenamon Mountain dominating to the NE. The view is impeded upslope to the S. A cairn (WA001-044----), though not visible from the standing stone, is located on the summit of the hill c. 1.6km to the SSW. Identified and reported by Aoibheann Lambe , 21 March 2018. A sandstone standing stone (basal dims. 0.8m x 0.47m; H 1.2m) with some quartz pebble inclusions, roughly rectangular in plan, aligned E-W and embedded in the ground. The top surface, which slopes upwards to the E, is quite smooth, possibly indicating the stone was originally taller and that at some stage the upper portion sheared off due to natural weathering. The broad faces narrow towards the top (top dims. 0.5m x 0.47m).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 16 April 2018

The N portal-stone (H 2.2m) and the N sidestone (H 1.7m) are undisturbed. (Borlase 1897, vol. 1, 56; Ó Nualláin 1983, 102)

WA002-065----:
Located on a gentle NE-facing slope, in pasture. Slievenamon is visible to the NNW, there is a low-lying ridge to the NE, very good view to E, impeded view upslope to the S but Comeragh Mountains visible over the crest of the hill, impeded to W by rise in slope though mountains are visible beyond. This is an Old Red Sandstone monolith with a rectangular cross-section (dims. 0.54m x 0.45m; H 1.05m) roughly aligned N-S. According to local information the stone remained upright until 2015. It has now fallen over and lies in the hollow where it formerly stood, resting on two grassy hummocks. The total length of stone (L 1.15m) suggests that only 0.1m of the stone was below ground as 1.05m was visible above the ground when the upright stone was recorded in 1989. However, the ground around the stone had been eroded by cattle by 0.1-0.15m. The bottom rectangular surface of the stone is very flat (dims. 0.37m x 0.34m).

On the 1st  (1941) ed. 6-inch OS map there is a ‘Ford & Footstick’ crossing the river, which had been replaced by a bridge by the 2nd (1925) ed. There are limited views from this standing stone as there is a steep rise in slope both on the N and S side of the river. The Comeragh Mountains are visible to the W, dominated by Knockanaffrin to the SW. Standing stone (H 1.83m; max. Wth 1.4m) of red conglomerate sandstone with quartz pebble inclusions. It is aligned E-W, with the broad N face (L 1.25m) facing the river. Roughly sub-rectangular in plan, though the S face (L 1.4m)  is not straight and the stone narrows from the W (Wth 0.63m) towards the E (Wth 0.15m). The stone also tapers (Wth 0.38m) as it rises. The top of the stone has broken off. The area around the standing stone has been poached by cattle resulting in a slight hollow. There is a possible packing stone (dims. c. 0.4m x 0.2m) at the W end of the S side. There is some evidence of attempts in the past to break the stone, evident from 3 drilling holes, one horizontal (L 0.21m) and two vertical (diam. 0.1m; D 0.04-0.05m), on the S face, c. 40m above the base of the stone.

WA017-035----:
Situated in scrub at the crest of a N-facing slope. This is an undifferentiated passage (L 3m; Wth 0.9m) oriented E-W with three sidestones on each side and one surviving lintel. A blocking-stone, two stones of a façade and outer-walling on the S side of the passage also survive. (Ó Nualláin and Walsh 1986, 26, 28) There is a large orthostat (dims. 2.45m x 0.7m; H 1.6m) NW of the wedge tomb. A field boundary runs immediately W of the tomb and dumped along the W side of this boundary for 22m N of the tomb and 9m to S there are small to medium sized stones from field clearance. These terminate 10m S of the tomb in a group of four large flat-sided boulders, one of which (dims. 2.1m x 0.7m; H 1.05m) is upright against the field boundary, one is lying against the field boundary  (2.6m x 1.3m x T 0.6m), one is partially resting on the former (2m x 1.5m x T 0.6m) and the third (2m x 1.3m x T 0.5m) is partially resting on this one.

WA027-007----:
Situated in rough pasture towards the S end of the summit of a N-S ridge. This is an undifferentiated passage (L 6.1m; Wth 1.05m at the entrance to 1.37m) opening to the ENE, composed of a sillstone with six sidestones on each side which increase in height towards the W backstone. The side-walls have outer support walls. Two of the original five lintels are in place. The passage is surrounded by a kerb of 27 stones (diam. 9.15m). It was first noted by Ryland (1824, 243), followed by the Halls (Scott 1984, 117-8), and described by Reade (1868-9) who called the ridge Carrick a Dhirra. Later commentators found it unchanged (Atkins 1896; Ó Nualláin and Walsh 1986, 25).
It was excavated in 1939 by J. Hawkes (1941) when the cremated remains of two individuals and a stone pendant were found in the passage, although it had previously been robbed-out (Reade 1868-9, 161-2). The covering cairn (diam. c. 15.25m) had spilled outside the orthostats, and it may have had an outer kerb of dispersed orthostats. The cairn contained secondary burials, all cremations, one with a bowl food vessel (Ó Ríordáin and Waddell 1993, 139), three with cordoned urns (Kavanagh 1976, 374-5), one of which had a pygmy cup (Kavanagh 1977), and an unclassifiable urn. The cremated remains of at least five others were found in two pits. Finds associated with the secondary burials consist of a razor, a faience bead and perforated bone pins.

The Comeragh Mountains are visible to the N, the estuary to the E where the River Brickey flows into the Dungarvan estuary, Helvick Head to ESE, there is a ridge of hills to the S which continues to the SW as Drum Hills. There is a concentration of dock weeds around the edge of the hollow. A standing stone had stood in this hollow until c. 2014 (ibid.). On the lower flat terrace of ridge running roughly E-W on S side of Licky river valley, in wet reclaimed grassland. Ground waterlogged immediately S of standing stone. The views are good to the N with  the Knockmealdown mountains visible in the distance, from N to E it is dominated by the ridge on the opposite side of the valley, poor E, limited S by rising ground and poor W along the ridge, with very good views to the NW. According to Power (1952, 96) Drumgallane, or Drum Galláin, means the hill of the Galláns or standing stones. He records that formerly two standing stones, one slender, the other rather thick were on the hill.  The standing stones (WA038-051----) mentioned by Power were previously unrecorded. However, in 2018 a standing stone was identified by Finbarr and Daragh Nolan at Drumgullane West which may be Power's 'rather thick' standing stone.
A sandstone standing stone (H 1.11m; 0.56mNW face; 0.83m SW face;  0.23m SE face; 1.06m NE face), aligned NW-SE, with the upper surface rising towards the NW. It has been badly spalled resulting in the erosion, particularly at ground level, of the S angle, giving the ground plan a triangular appearance, however, at a slightly higher level the sub-rectangular plan of the stone is more evident. The NE side appears to have fractured, the present face appears to be the result of a clear vertical split. There are a lot of field clearance stones around the base of the standing stone, particularly to the NE and SW. There is a mound of field clearance stones c. 28m SE of the standing stone which  is heavily overgrown with brambles.
